y: From ā- + *bielġan.
From Proto-West Germanic *balgijan.
From Proto-Germanic *hūlōną. Cognate with Old High German hūilōn, Old Norse úla.

s: a wooden board with a low rim; tray
y:
From trauj-, from trauwʲ-, the oblique stem of Proto-West Germanic *trawi, from Proto-Germanic *trawją (“wooden vessel”). Cognate with Old Swedish trø (“wooden grain measure”), Low German Treechel (“dough trough”), possibly Old Norse treyja (“carrier”). Related to Old English trog (“trough”).
Thought to be from the same root as trēow (“tree”), from Proto-Germanic *trewą, from Proto-Indo-European *dóru (“tree”), *drew- (“hard, firm, strong, solid”). Potential cognates from this root include Sanskrit द्रोण (droṇa, “trough”) and Ancient Greek δροίτη (droítē, “tub, vat”).
For the phonetic development, compare hīeġ and īeġ.

s: used to form the nominative singular n-stem (weak) adjective and subsequent nominalised form
used to form masculine agents, usually from verbs
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-ō, from Proto-Germanic *-ô. Cognate with Old High German -o.
From Proto-West Germanic *-ō, from Proto-Germanic *-ô.

s: Forms the nominative, accusative, and genitive plural of o-stem feminine nouns and u-stem masculine nouns
Forms the genitive plural of a-stem nouns
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-ō, from Proto-Germanic *-ǫ̂, from the Proto-Indo-European genitive plural ending *-oHom as attached to thematic (eh₂-stem and o-stem) nouns.

s: Forms the genitive and dative singular of u-stem nouns
used to form the infinitive of most strong, class 1 weak, and preterite-present verbs (exceptions are verbs like flēon (“to flee”))
y: From Proto-Germanic *-aną and Proto-Germanic *-janą.
From Proto-West Germanic *-anā, from Proto-Germanic *-anē.

s: Forms the accusative, genitive, and dative singular and nominative and accusative plural of n-stem nouns
y:
Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-an, from a conflation of several Proto-Germanic n-stem suffixes: *-anų (accusative singular), *-aniz (genitive singular, nominative/vocative plural) and *-anunz (accusative plural).
Supplanted Proto-West Germanic *-ōn during the prehistory of Old English except for in relic forms such as ēastron and foldu.

s: alternative form of -on (strong plural past indicative suffix)
Masculine and feminine accusative, genitive, dative, and instrumental singular
Neuter genitive, dative, and instrumental singular
Masculine, feminine, and neuter nominative and accusative plural

y: From -enne, with the first /e/ shifting due to influence from -an.

s: Plural ending of nominative and accusative cases, originally of a-stem masculine nouns, later extended to other nouns.
y: Perhaps from the Proto-Germanic accusative plural ending *-anz, with regularly lost -n- before a fricative, or perhaps from the nominative plural *-ōs, a voiceless variety of the regular ending *-ōz, or a merger of both. Akin to Saterland Frisian -s, West Frisian -s, Old Saxon -os (Low German -s), Dutch -s, Swedish -ar.

s: alternative form of -ast; marks the second person singular present indicative of class II weak verbs
Used to form the second person singular present indicative of class II weak verbs
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-ōs with paragogic -t added from when þū follows (compare Anglian Old English -as), from Proto-Germanic *-ōsi, from Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yési.

s: Third person singular present indicative ending of class 2 weak verbs.
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-ōþ, from Proto-Germanic *-ōþi.

s: First, second and third person plural present indicative ending of strong verbs, class 1 weak verbs, and class 3 weak verbs.
Second person plural imperative ending of strong verbs, class 1 weak verbs, and class 3 weak verbs.
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-anþ (“third person plural indicative ending of weak verbs”), from Proto-Germanic *-anþi (“third person plural indicative ending of weak verbs”). Cognate with Old Saxon -ad, Swabian -ad.
From Proto-West Germanic *-blōdī. Equivalent to blōd + -e. Cognate with Old High German -bluoti.
From the verb beran.

s: having the qualities of, characterized by
y: From Proto-Germanic *bēriz (“bearing, carrying”). Akin to Old Frisian -ber, Old Saxon -bāri, and Old High German -bāri.

s: Creates masculine concrete nouns (including proper nouns) from adjectives, verbs, or other nouns, usually typifying a condition or state, or characterising a diminutive aspect.
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-ukō, from Proto-Germanic *-ukô, equivalent to -oc + -a.

s: suffix forming diminutives from nouns, often displaying i-mutation
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-ikīn, *-ukīn, equivalent to -oc + -en. Cognate with Old Norse -ki. More at -kin.

s: suffix applied to verbs and deverbal nouns to form other verbs with an intensive or frequentative force
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-ukōn, *-ikōn, from Proto-Germanic *-ukōną, *-ikōną. Cognate with Old Frisian -kia, Old Saxon -akōn, Old High German -ichōn, Old Norse -ka.
Identical to the noun cræft (“art, skill, strength”).

s: suffix denoting origin, derivation, or likeness
feorran (“from far away”) + -cund → feorrancund (“come from afar”)
y: From Proto-Germanic *kundaz (“born, natured”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₁tós. Cognate with Old Norse -kundr, Gothic -𐌺𐌿𐌽𐌳𐍃 (-kunds).

s: used to form the first and third person singular preterite indicative of some class I and class III weak verbs

y: From Proto-West Germanic *-dōm, from Proto-Germanic *-dōmaz.
From West Germanic *-ā, from Proto-Germanic *-ê, which survives otherwise only in Gothic (and possibly Old Norse).

s: forms adjectives from nouns, often with the meaning "having" (typically causes i-umlaut)
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-ī. Beyond that, generally from Proto-Germanic *-ijaz, but also partly merged with *-jaz and athematic *-iz (compare Proto-Norse -ᛁᛉ (-iʀ)). Note though that -wintre is from Proto-Germanic *-wintruz, since Proto-Germanic u-stem adjectives became ja-stems in West Germanic. Other suffixes derived from u-stem nouns, such as -flēre, might also have been zero derivations in Proto-Germanic.

s: Used to form the first person singular present indicative of strong verbs and class I weak verbs
y: Likely borrowed from the subjunctive singular Proto-West Germanic *-ē after high vowel apocope resulted in the loss of inherited Proto-West Germanic *-u in heavy stem verbs, and then analogically extended to light stem verbs.

s: Marks the dative singular of a-stem and ō-stem nouns
sċip (“ship”) + -e → tō þām sċipe (“to the ship”)
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-ē, from Proto-Germanic *-ai (a-stem), *-ōi (ō-stem), from the Proto-Indo-European dative singular ending *-ey or locative singular ending *-i as attached to eh₂-stem and o-stem nouns.

s: Marks the accusative and genitive and the nominative and accusative plural of ō-stem feminine nouns
y:
A combination of multiple sources:
* In the accusative singular, from Proto-West Germanic *-ā, from Proto-Germanic *-ǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *-ā́m, from *-eh₂ (eh₂-stem suffix) + *-m (accusative singular suffix).
* In the genitive singular, from Proto-West Germanic *-ā, from Proto-Germanic *-ōz, from Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂s, from *-eh₂ (eh₂-stem suffix) + *-s (genitive singular suffix).
* In the accusative plural, from Proto-West Germanic *-ā, from Proto-Germanic *-ōz, from Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂m̥s, from *-eh₂ (eh₂-stem suffix) + *-ms (accusative plural suffix).
This suffix was extended to the nominative plural (replacing -a < Proto-West Germanic *-ō) in Old English itself.

s: Marks the nominative singular of feminine n-stem nouns
Forms feminine agent nouns, often as a counterpart to masculine agent nouns in -a
ġebedda (“husband, male consort”) + -e → ġebedde (“wife, female consort”)
Forms nouns referring to female people from nouns referring to male people
Second person plural imperative ending of strong verbs, class 1 weak verbs, and class 3 weak verbs.
y: Likely derived from the weakening of the plural subjunctive ending -en.

s: Used to form the past participle of class I weak verbs
suffix applied to nouns meaning "having", "possessing", "provided with" or "equipped with"
y: Akin to the past participle ending -ed.

s: Used to form the first and third person singular preterite indicative of most class I weak verbs
Used to form the second person singular preterite indicative of class I weak verbs
Used to form the plural preterite indicative of class I weak verbs

y: From Proto-Germanic *-a-l-.

s: agent and instrumental suffix creating nouns from verbs
y: From Proto-Germanic *-ilaz.

s: suffix forming nouns denoting process or action from verbs
house; dwelling, building, variant of botl
y: Possibly a metathetic variant of earlier Proto-Germanic *-þlą.
A metathetic form of Proto-West Germanic *-islī.
A metathetic form of Proto-West Germanic *-islī.

s: used to create diminutive neuter nouns
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-īn, from Proto-Germanic *-īną.

s: used to create feminine nouns from other nouns
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-ini, from Proto-Germanic *-inī.

s: adjectival suffix meaning "material made of, consisting of”, also sometimes “characteristic of”.
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-īn, from Proto-Germanic *-īnaz.

s: past participle ending of strong verbs
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-an, from Proto-Germanic *-anaz.

s: meaning belonging to or characterised by
tungol (“star”) + -en → tunglen (“of the stars, sidereal, starry”)
y: Proto-Germanic *-an, from Proto-Germanic *-an-.

s: forms nouns from class 1 weak verbs
þicgan (“to take, accept”) + -en → þigen (“taking”) (inflected as strong and weak)
y: Inherited from Proto-Germanic *-īni, from Proto-Germanic *-īniz. Sometimes with geminate -nn-, probably due to confusion with the feminine suffix from *-inī.

s: forms the genitive plural of n-stem masculine, n-stem feminine, and some ō-stem feminine nouns

s: forms the weak genitive plural of adjectives
y: (This etymology is missing or incomplete. Please add to it, or discuss it at the Etymology scriptorium. )

s: suffix denoting the agent of an action; -er
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-andi, from Proto-Germanic *-andz, taken from the present participle form of verbs. See -ende.

s: equivalent of English -ing; suffix for present participles
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-andī, from Proto-Germanic *-andz. Akin to Latin -āns, -ēns; Ancient Greek -ων (-ōn), Persian ـنده (-ande).
From Proto-Germanic *-andiją. Compare Old Norse -indi.
See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

s: forming adjectives from verbs with the sense of "able to, capable of"; -able
y: Combined form, created from -ende (present participle ending) + -līċ (“-ly, like”) and from -end (agent suffix, ultimately from the present participle) + -līċ (“-ly, like”). Equivalent to -andly in modern English.
See -enne.
See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

s: Forms the inflected infinitive of verbs.
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-annjē, dative inflection of the infinitive -an; equivalent to -an + -e

s: masculine agent suffix, originally applied only to nouns
y:
From Proto-West Germanic *-ārī, from Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz.
Uncertain ultimate origin, usually held to be from Latin -ārius. Gąsiorowski instead suggests that *-ārijaz is a native formation; he derives it from earlier *-azrijaz, which he etymologises as a zero-grade form of *-sōr suffixed with *-ih₂, creating a suffix *-sr-ih₂ for forming feminine agent nouns, which were then masculinised by attaching *-ós. He also suggests a relation to Proto-West Germanic *-astrijā.
Cognate with Old Frisian -ere, Old Saxon -āri, Old High German -āri.

s: A frequentative suffix used to form verbs
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-urōn (frequentative suffix), from Proto-Germanic *-urōną. Cognate with Old High German -arōn.
From the adjectival use of -ærn (“noun suffix denoting location”), from ærn (“place”).

s: Suffix meaning "toward a place"; alternative form of -erne
y: Variant of -erne.

s: Adjective suffix occurring in names for directions
y: Akin to Old High German -rōni; see -ern for more.

s: genitive case/possessive marker for a-stem nouns, indicating that an object belongs to the noun
forms the strong masculine/neuter genitive singular of adjectives
used in formation of adverbs, originally from the genitive of masculine and neuter nouns, but later added also to feminine nouns by analogy
y: The a-stem genitive singular ending is derived from Proto-West Germanic *-as, from Proto-Germanic *-as. Based on the voiceless *s, Ringe 2006 argues that this ending was analogically taken from the genitive singular determiner *þas, from *tósyo.

s: Alternative form of -est; marks the second person singular of class I weak verbs
suffix forming feminine nouns, originally from verbs
y: From Proto-Germanic *-ustaz, *-istaz.

s: alternative form of -ost (“used to form superlative adjectives and adverbs”)
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-ist, from Proto-Germanic *-istaz, from Proto-Indo-European *-istos, from *-yōs + *-tHós.

s: Forms the second-person singular of class I weak verbs
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-ēs with paragogic -t added from when þū follows (compare Anglian Old English -es), from Proto-Germanic *-ēz (with -s by analogy with present forms), from Proto-Indo-European *-eh₁si (in *dʰédʰeh₁si, form of *dʰédʰeh₁ti).

s: female agent suffix, especially denoting one who is skilled in a particular occupation or craft
bæcestre (“female baker”); sangestre (“female singer”); webbestre (“female weaver”)
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-astrijā, feminine agent suffix equivalent to *-ārī (> -ere).

s: suffix forming nouns from verbs, adjectives, and other nouns (sometimes causing i-mutation), originally as the action of verbs ending in -ettan (“-ise”) (compare English -ism)
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-ati, *-iti, *-uti, from Proto-Germanic *-atją, *-itją, *-utją.

s: used to form verbs from nouns or adjectives (compare English -ate, -ize), frequently having a causative force.
verbal suffix denoting frequency or intensification
hlēapan (“to jump, to leap”) + -ettan → hlēapettan (“to jump up”)
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-attjan, *-ittjan, *-uttjan, from Proto-Germanic *-atjaną, *-itjaną, *-utjaną (verbal suffix). Related to English -ise.

s: Third person singular present indicative ending of class 1 weak verbs
suffix denoting multiplication, or consisting of so many parts; -fold
y:
From Proto-West Germanic *-falþ, from Proto-Germanic *-falþaz (“-fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *poltos (“-fold”).
Cognate with Old Frisian -fald, Old Saxon -fald, German -falt, Old Norse -faldr, Gothic -𐍆𐌰𐌻𐌸𐍃 (-falþs).
